title: Methods & Receivers
summary: A **method** is just a function with a special **receiver** argument bound to a type: `func (c *Counter) Inc()`. The single most important decision is the receiver kind — a **value receiver** operates on a *copy* (mutations don't persist), while a **pointer receiver** operates on the *original* (mutations persist). Get this right and methods feel obvious; get it wrong and your updates silently vanish.

subtopics.title: A method is a function with a receiver
subtopics.explanation: A method is declared like a function but with an extra parameter — the receiver — written in parentheses before the name. `func (c Counter) Value() int` reads as 'a method Value on Counter', and calling `c.Value()` is sugar for binding c as that receiver. You can only define methods on types declared in the same package. This receiver argument is the whole basis of how methods bind behavior to a type.

subtopics.title: Value receiver gets a copy
subtopics.explanation: A value receiver (`func (c Counter)`) receives a COPY of the value. Any mutation inside the method changes the copy and is lost when the method returns. Value receivers are for reading, not writing — ideal for small, immutable-by-intent types. Choosing a value receiver is one half of the receiver-kind decision at the heart of this topic.

subtopics.title: Pointer receiver mutates the original
subtopics.explanation: A pointer receiver (`func (c *Counter)`) receives the address of the value, so the method operates on the original and mutations persist after the method returns. Use a pointer receiver whenever the method needs to change the value, or when copying the value would be expensive. Picking a pointer receiver is the other half of the receiver decision this topic is built around.

subtopics.title: Method sets & interface satisfaction
subtopics.explanation: The method set of T contains only its value-receiver methods, while the method set of *T contains BOTH value- and pointer-receiver methods. So if any method has a pointer receiver, only *T satisfies an interface that requires it — a plain T value does not. This links receiver choice directly to which types can be used as methods' interface implementations.

subtopics.title: Automatic addressing & dereferencing
subtopics.explanation: On an ADDRESSABLE value, Go inserts the address-of/dereference for you: `c.Inc()` becomes `(&c).Inc()` automatically. But you cannot call a pointer-receiver method on a non-addressable value such as a map element or a literal — there's no address to take. This convenience is why pointer-receiver methods feel as natural to call as value-receiver ones.

subtopics.title: Methods on any defined type
subtopics.explanation: You can attach methods to ANY defined type in your package, not just structs — including a named type over a built-in like `type Celsius float64`. You cannot add methods to types from other packages or to built-in types directly; define a local named type first. This shows that methods and receivers apply to the whole type system, not only to structs.

subtopics.title: Method values & method expressions
subtopics.explanation: A method bound to a receiver can be stored as a first-class function value: `f := c.Inc` captures c and calls the method when invoked, while a method expression `Counter.Value` yields a function whose first argument is the receiver. Method values are how you pass a method around like a callback. This rounds out the receiver story: a method is a function, so it can be a value too.

foundations.overview: Go has no classes, but it lets you attach behavior to data by declaring methods — functions with a receiver argument bound to a named type. The deepest decision you make is the receiver kind. A value receiver works on a copy, so it can read but not durably mutate; a pointer receiver works on the original, so its changes stick. Almost every 'my struct update isn't saving' bug in Go traces back to accidentally using a value receiver. Master receivers and you understand how Go models objects, interfaces, and mutation.
foundations.formalDefinition: A method is a function with a receiver: a single named parameter, of type T or *T (where T is a defined type in the same package), declared between the func keyword and the method name. The method is in the method set of its receiver type and is invoked with selector syntax value.Method(args).
foundations.whyItMatters: Receivers decide whether your changes persist, which types satisfy which interfaces, and how much copying happens on every call. It is the gateway concept to interfaces, encapsulation, and idiomatic API design in Go — and a guaranteed interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a value receiver as handing the method a photocopy of a document: it can scribble on the copy, but your original is untouched. A pointer receiver hands over the original document itself, so anything it writes is permanent. Choosing the receiver is choosing whether the method gets the copy or the real thing.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A method call is compiled essentially into a function call where the receiver is the first argument: t.M(x) becomes (roughly) M(t, x). With a value receiver the compiler copies the receiver onto the call stack; with a pointer receiver it passes an 8-byte pointer. For an addressable operand the compiler auto-inserts &t or *t so the call type-checks; for a non-addressable operand (map element, literal, return value) it cannot take an address, so a pointer-receiver call is rejected.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Mutating state on structs (counters, buffers, connection pools), implementing interfaces (io.Writer's Write has a pointer receiver), defining behavior on domain types (Money.Add, Duration.Hours), and giving named primitive types formatting (Celsius.String).
foundations.businessImpact: Correct receiver choice prevents an entire class of silent data-loss bugs where state updates appear to succeed but never persist — bugs that are expensive to find in production financial or inventory code.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Consistent receiver kinds make a type's API predictable and make interface satisfaction obvious. Mixing value and pointer receivers on the same type is a well-known smell that confuses callers and breaks interface assignment.
foundations.performanceImpact: A value receiver on a large struct copies every field on every call, adding CPU and allocation pressure in hot paths. A pointer receiver passes one word. But a value receiver on a tiny type can be faster and avoids heap escapes.
commonUseCases: Pointer receivers to mutate struct state (Inc, Push, SetName)
Value receivers for small read-only types (Point.Dist, Celsius.ToF)
Implementing interfaces like fmt.Stringer or io.Writer
Methods on named primitive types (type Celsius float64)

commonMisconceptions.myth: A value-receiver method can mutate the struct it's called on.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It mutates a copy. The original is unchanged once the method returns. Use a pointer receiver to persist mutations.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must write &c to call a pointer-receiver method.
commonMisconceptions.reality: On an addressable value Go inserts the address-of automatically: c.Inc() becomes (&c).Inc(). You only need an explicit pointer when the value isn't addressable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Methods can only be defined on structs.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can define methods on any defined type in the package, including named types over primitives like type Celsius float64 — just not on types from other packages.

visualExplorer.title: What happens on a pointer-receiver call
visualExplorer.caption: Calling a pointer-receiver method on an addressable value: Go takes the address, the method mutates through it, and the caller sees the change.

config.intro: Step through `c.Inc()` where `func (c *Counter) Inc()` mutates the receiver:

steps.name: Resolve the receiver kind
steps.detail: Inc is declared with a pointer receiver `*Counter`, so the call needs a *Counter, but `c` is a plain Counter value.

steps.name: Automatic addressing
steps.detail: Because `c` is addressable (a local variable), the compiler rewrites `c.Inc()` to `(&c).Inc()` — it takes the address for you.

steps.name: Pass the pointer
steps.detail: The method receives an 8-byte pointer to the real `c`, not a copy of its fields.

steps.name: Mutate through the pointer
steps.detail: `c.n++` inside the method writes to the original Counter's memory.

steps.name: Caller sees the change
steps.detail: Control returns and `c` now reflects the increment — contrast with a value receiver, which would have mutated a discarded copy.

interactiveExamples.title: Value vs pointer receiver, side by side
interactiveExamples.explanation: IncCopy uses a value receiver, so it bumps a copy and the change is lost. IncReal uses a pointer receiver, so the increment persists. This is the single most important behavior to internalize about receivers.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the deposit stick
interactiveExamples.explanation: Deposit is meant to add money to the account, but balances never change. Fix the receiver so the mutation persists, then the final balance should be 150.

checkpoints.explanation: Set has a VALUE receiver, so it mutates a copy of b. The original b.v stays 1. A pointer receiver `func (b *Box) Set` would have printed 99.

checkpoints.prompt: A method `func (c *Counter) Inc()` has a pointer receiver. Which is in the method set of the VALUE type Counter (not *Counter)?
options: Only value-receiver methods; Inc is NOT in Counter's method set
Neither — method sets only apply to interfaces
checkpoints.explanation: The method set of T contains only value-receiver methods. Pointer-receiver methods belong to *T's method set. So Inc is in *Counter's set but not Counter's — which is why only *Counter can satisfy an interface requiring Inc.

options: A map element is not addressable, so Go can't take its address for the pointer receiver
checkpoints.explanation: Pointer-receiver calls require an addressable operand so Go can take &operand. Map elements are not addressable, so m["a"].Inc() is a compile error. Fix it by pulling the value out, mutating it, and putting it back, or by storing *C in the map.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the receiver so Push durably appends to the stack.
checkpoints.explanation: Push reassigns s.items, a mutation that must persist, so it needs a pointer receiver `s *Stack`. A value receiver would append to a copy's slice header and lose the change.

codeLab.title: Implement a Stack with correct receivers
codeLab.instructions: Complete the Stack type. Push(x) appends an element; Pop() removes and returns the top with an ok flag (false if empty); Len() returns the count. Mutating methods must use pointer receivers so changes persist; read-only methods may use a value receiver.
hints: Push and Pop change s.items, so they MUST use pointer receivers or the changes vanish.
Pop the top by reading s.items[len-1] then re-slicing to s.items[:len-1]; guard the empty case with ok=false.
Len only reads, so a value receiver is fine — but a pointer receiver would also work and is fine for consistency.

debuggingLab.title: The rename never sticks
debuggingLab.symptom: After calling SetName, the user's name is still the old value.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: SetName has a VALUE receiver (u User), so the method operates on a copy of u. Assigning u.name = n changes that copy, which is discarded when the method returns. The caller's u is never touched, so the name stays "old". This is the classic 'my setter doesn't work' Go bug.
commonMistakes: Using a value receiver for a method that is supposed to mutate state.
Assuming u.SetName(...) passes the original because the call uses dot syntax — it still copies for a value receiver.
Mixing value and pointer receivers on the same type, which makes the mutation behavior inconsistent and surprising.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Change SetName to use a pointer receiver so the assignment mutates the real User.

theory.question: What is the difference between a value receiver and a pointer receiver?
theory.directAnswer: A value receiver (func (t T)) receives a copy of the value, so mutations inside the method don't affect the caller's value. A pointer receiver (func (t *T)) receives the address, so the method operates on the original and mutations persist. Use a pointer receiver when the method mutates state or when copying the value would be expensive; use a value receiver for small read-only types.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to bind a method to a type — by copy or by reference.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go needs an explicit, visible choice between mutating the original and operating on a copy, with no hidden 'this' semantics.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The receiver is compiled as the method's first argument; a value receiver copies the value onto the stack, a pointer receiver passes one word and reads/writes through it.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong causes silent data-loss bugs (mutations on a copy) and affects which interfaces a type satisfies — a near-guaranteed interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: bytes.Buffer's Write uses a pointer receiver so writes accumulate; a small Point's Add can use a value receiver because copying two ints is trivial.

followUps.question: When would you prefer a pointer receiver even if the method doesn't mutate?
followUps.answer: When the struct is large (to avoid copying every call) or for consistency, since mixing receiver kinds on one type is discouraged.

followUps.question: Can a value receiver ever change something visible to the caller?
followUps.answer: Only indirectly — if a field is a pointer, map, or slice header that shares an underlying object, the copy still points at the same data; but reassigning the field itself won't persist.

theory.question: Explain method sets and why only *T sometimes satisfies an interface.
theory.directAnswer: The method set of T contains only its value-receiver methods; the method set of *T contains both value- and pointer-receiver methods. An interface is satisfied only if the concrete type's method set includes all the interface's methods. So if any required method has a pointer receiver, a plain T value does NOT satisfy the interface — only *T (or &t) does.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The set of methods callable on a given type, which determines interface satisfaction.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because you can't always take the address of a value (it may be non-addressable), pointer-receiver methods can't be guaranteed callable on a bare T, so they're excluded from T's method set.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interface assignment checks the static method set: assigning t (type T) to an interface requiring a pointer-receiver method fails to compile; assigning &t (type *T) succeeds.

theory.whyImportant: It explains confusing 'does not implement interface (method has pointer receiver)' compile errors that trip up many Go developers.
theory.realWorldExample: If (*T).Read satisfies io.Reader but Read has a pointer receiver, you must pass &t, not t, where an io.Reader is expected.

followUps.question: Why is taking &t inside a method call usually fine but not for interface satisfaction?
followUps.answer: For a direct call the operand is often addressable so Go auto-takes the address; but interface satisfaction is a static type-level check on the method set, where no addressing is implied.

theory.question: What is a method value versus a method expression, and how do they differ?
theory.directAnswer: A method value binds a specific receiver at the point you take it: `f := c.Inc` captures c, so calling `f()` invokes Inc on that captured c with no argument. A method expression leaves the receiver unbound: `g := (*Counter).Inc` yields a plain function whose FIRST argument is the receiver, so you call `g(&c)`. Method values are for passing a bound method as a callback; method expressions are for treating the method generically over any receiver.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to turn a method into a first-class function value — one with the receiver pre-bound, one with the receiver as an explicit parameter.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Since a method is just a function with a receiver argument, Go lets you either freeze that argument (method value) or expose it (method expression), so methods integrate with Go's first-class function support.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: `c.Inc` evaluates c immediately and stores it in a closure; the resulting func's signature drops the receiver. `T.M` or `(*T).M` keeps the receiver as the leading parameter, giving a func(recv, args...) you invoke by passing the receiver explicitly.

theory.whyImportant: Method values are how you register a method as an event handler or goroutine body, and getting the receiver-capture timing right avoids subtle bugs when the receiver changes after capture.
theory.realWorldExample: Passing `timer.Stop` (a method value bound to a *time.Timer) into a defer, or wiring `handler.ServeHTTP` as an http.HandlerFunc, both rely on method values carrying their receiver.

followUps.question: When you write f := c.Inc with a pointer-receiver Inc, is the receiver copied?
followUps.answer: The pointer is captured. If c is a value, Go captures &c (c must be addressable); subsequent mutations through f affect the same underlying c.

followUps.question: How does a method expression help with generic-style dispatch?
followUps.answer: Because the receiver is an ordinary parameter, you can store several method expressions in a slice or map and call them uniformly by passing different receivers.

theory.question: Why can Go call a pointer-receiver method on a plain variable without you writing &, and when does that automatic addressing fail?
theory.directAnswer: For an ADDRESSABLE operand, the compiler rewrites `c.Inc()` into `(&c).Inc()` automatically, so you rarely write & yourself. It fails when the operand is NOT addressable — map elements, literals like `Counter{}.Inc()`, and function/method return values — because there is no stable address for Go to take, producing a compile error.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The compiler's implicit insertion of address-of (and dereference) so selector syntax works regardless of receiver kind.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It keeps calling code uniform — you use value.Method() the same way whether the method has a value or pointer receiver — without forcing callers to reason about addressing on every call.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: During type checking, if a pointer-receiver method is called on an addressable value, Go inserts &operand; if a value-receiver method is called on a pointer, it inserts *operand. Addressability is a static property: local variables, slice elements, and dereferenced pointers are addressable; map elements and temporaries are not.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding addressability explains a whole family of otherwise-cryptic compile errors and clarifies why some fixes (pull-out-and-write-back, or store pointers) are necessary.
theory.realWorldExample: `m["k"].Inc()` on a map[string]Counter fails to compile because the map element isn't addressable, whereas `s[0].Inc()` on a []Counter compiles fine because slice elements are addressable.

followUps.question: Is a struct field of a local variable addressable?
followUps.answer: Yes — if the struct itself is addressable, so are its fields, so you can call pointer-receiver methods on them directly.

followUps.question: Why is a value returned from a function not addressable?
followUps.answer: It lives in a temporary with no guaranteed storage location, so &result is illegal; assign it to a variable first to make it addressable.

scenario.question: A teammate stores structs in a map and calls a pointer-receiver method directly on a map element, and it won't compile. What's wrong and what are the fixes?
scenario.directAnswer: Map elements are not addressable, so Go can't synthesize &m[key] to satisfy the pointer receiver — hence the compile error. Fix it by copying the value out, mutating it, and writing it back (v := m[k]; v.Method(); m[k] = v), or by storing pointers in the map (map[K]*T) so each element already is a pointer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A non-addressability constraint on pointer-receiver method calls.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Map internals may move entries, so the language forbids taking the address of a map element, which a pointer receiver would require.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For addressable operands Go inserts &operand; for non-addressable ones (map elements, literals, function results) it can't, so the call is rejected at compile time.

scenario.whyImportant: It's a common real-world stumbling block when modeling mutable entities in maps.
scenario.realWorldExample: A cache stored as map[string]Session where SessionTouch() has a pointer receiver fails to compile; switching to map[string]*Session fixes it and avoids copy-back boilerplate.

followUps.question: Why does the same call work on a slice element but not a map element?
followUps.answer: Slice elements are addressable (the backing array has a stable address), so &s[i] is legal and Go can auto-address; map elements are not.

scenario.question: In code review you find one type where some methods use value receivers and others use pointer receivers. Callers report that the type sometimes fails to satisfy an interface. Why, and how do you fix it cleanly?
scenario.directAnswer: Mixing receiver kinds makes the type's behavior and method set inconsistent: the method set of the value type T only includes the value-receiver methods, so if the interface needs a pointer-receiver method, a bare T value silently fails to satisfy it (only *T does). Fix it by standardizing on one receiver kind — for any type with mutable state, make ALL methods pointer receivers — so the type is used consistently via *T and interface satisfaction is predictable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A consistency problem where a single type's methods split across value and pointer receivers, fragmenting its method sets.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go allows per-method receiver choice, but interface satisfaction depends on the full method set of the exact type (T vs *T), so a mixed set produces surprising satisfaction rules.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: If any required method has a pointer receiver, only *T's method set contains everything the interface needs; T's does not. Assigning a value T where the interface is expected then fails to compile, while &t works — an inconsistency that looks arbitrary to callers.

scenario.whyImportant: This is a classic maintainability and correctness smell; standardizing receiver kinds removes an entire category of confusing compile errors and copy-vs-original ambiguity.
scenario.realWorldExample: A Service type had Load() with a value receiver and Save() with a pointer receiver; passing a Service value where a Persister interface was expected failed, while passing &svc worked. The team converted all methods to pointer receivers and added a linter rule forbidding mixed receivers.

followUps.question: Is there any case where a value receiver is still right on a mutable type?
followUps.answer: Rarely — a purely read-only helper could be a value receiver, but for consistency and to avoid method-set surprises most teams make it a pointer receiver too once any method mutates.

followUps.question: How can you catch this automatically?
followUps.answer: Static-analysis tooling and go vet-style linters can flag types with mixed receiver kinds, and copylocks catches copying types that embed a sync.Mutex.

systemDesign.question: You are designing the public API for a shared, mutable connection-pool type used across many goroutines. How do receiver choices shape the design for correctness, safety, and performance?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Make the pool a pointer type: give every method a pointer receiver so mutations to internal state (idle list, counters) persist on the single shared instance and callers all reference the same pool. Guard shared state with a sync.Mutex accessed through those pointer-receiver methods, document that the pool must never be copied (a copied mutex is a bug go vet flags), and expose it through an interface whose method set matches *Pool so only pointers satisfy it. This keeps mutation correct, sharing safe, and avoids copying a large struct on every call.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An API-shape decision where receiver kind is the primary lever controlling mutation semantics, sharing, and copy cost for a stateful, concurrent type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A connection pool has mutable internal state that many goroutines must observe consistently; value receivers would copy that state per call, breaking both mutation persistence and shared visibility.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: All methods take *Pool, so calls operate on the one heap-allocated pool; a mutex field serializes access to the idle list and counters. Because pointer-receiver methods live only in *Pool's method set, any interface (e.g. Getter/Putter) is satisfied by *Pool, steering callers toward pointers and preventing accidental value copies.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Getting the receiver kind wrong here causes silent data loss (updates on copies) and data races (goroutines mutating separate copies or an unsynchronized shared one) — high-severity production bugs.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: database/sql's *DB and sync.Pool are pointer types with pointer-receiver methods and internal locking; they are documented as safe for concurrent use and must not be copied after first use.

followUps.question: How do you prevent callers from copying the pool?
followUps.answer: Return and accept *Pool everywhere, embed a noCopy or sync.Mutex so go vet's copylocks flags copies, and document that the zero value must be used by pointer.

followUps.question: What if some read-only method could be a value receiver for speed?
followUps.answer: On a large, shared, mutable type you still use a pointer receiver: a value copy would snapshot stale state and defeat sharing, so consistency and correctness outweigh a micro-optimization.

coding.question: Define a named type `type Celsius float64` with methods `ToF() Fahrenheit` and `String() string`, demonstrating methods on a non-struct type. Implement func Convert(c Celsius) string returning the String() form.
coding.thoughtProcess: Methods can attach to any defined type, including a named float. ToF reads the receiver and returns a converted value, so a value receiver is correct (it's small and immutable). String formats it. Convert just calls c.String(). No pointers needed because nothing mutates.
coding.lineByLine: Celsius and Fahrenheit are named types over float64, so they can carry methods. ToF computes the conversion and casts to the Fahrenheit type. String uses Sprintf with a degree symbol and implements fmt.Stringer, so Celsius prints nicely anywhere. Convert simply delegates to String. All receivers are values because the type is small and read-only.

followUps.question: Could you define these methods in a different package?
followUps.answer: No — you can only define methods on a type declared in the same package, so Celsius's methods must live where Celsius is declared.

followUps.question: Why use a value receiver here instead of a pointer?
followUps.answer: Celsius is a single float64 — copying is trivial and there's no mutation, so a value receiver is idiomatic and avoids unnecessary indirection.

coding.question: Define a Counter type with an Inc() method that durably increments, and a Value() method that reads the count. Then write func BumpAll(cs []Counter) that increments every counter in the slice in place. Explain which receivers you pick and why the slice mutation persists.
coding.thoughtProcess: Inc mutates state, so it needs a pointer receiver or the increment is lost on a copy. Value only reads, so a value receiver is fine (though a pointer receiver would also work). For BumpAll, slice elements are addressable, so cs[i].Inc() auto-takes &cs[i] and mutates the element in the backing array in place — no copy-back needed. Ranging by value (for _, c := range cs) would instead copy each element, so I index explicitly.
coding.lineByLine: Counter holds a single int field n. Inc has a pointer receiver *Counter so c.n++ writes to the original and persists. Value has a value receiver because it only reads. In BumpAll, ranging with an index (for i := range cs) lets us call cs[i].Inc(); because slice elements are addressable, Go rewrites this to (&cs[i]).Inc(), mutating the element inside the backing array. Ranging by value instead would copy each Counter, so the increments would be lost.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the number of counters
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra — mutation is in place

followUps.question: Why not use for _, c := range cs { c.Inc() }?
followUps.answer: That binds c to a COPY of each element; even with a pointer receiver Go takes the address of the copy, so the backing slice is never updated. Index with cs[i] to mutate in place.

followUps.question: Would BumpAll(cs []*Counter) change anything?
followUps.answer: It would also work — each element is already a pointer, so cs[i].Inc() dereferences it directly; but it forces callers to hold a slice of pointers rather than values.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Pick one receiver kind per type and stick to it: if any method needs a pointer receiver (most do, once a type has mutable state), make them all pointer receivers for a consistent, predictable API. Document whether a type is meant to be used as a value or always via a pointer.
productionDeepDive.performance: Value receivers copy the whole struct on every call; for large structs in hot paths that copy is real CPU and can force heap escapes. Prefer pointer receivers for big types. Conversely, tiny value types (a few words) are often cheaper by value and stay on the stack.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Pointer receivers expose the same underlying value to multiple goroutines, so mutating methods need synchronization (a mutex field, often itself accessed via pointer receiver). Value receivers give each goroutine its own copy but then can't share state — choose deliberately.
productionDeepDive.reliability: A nil pointer receiver is legal and a method can handle it gracefully (e.g. a nil *List behaving as empty); but dereferencing a nil receiver field panics. Decide and document whether your pointer-receiver methods tolerate a nil receiver.
productionDeepDive.observability: When wrapping types to add metrics or logging, keep receiver kinds aligned with the wrapped type so interface satisfaction (e.g. http.Handler, io.Writer) doesn't silently break at the wrapper boundary.
productionDeepDive.security: For value types that carry secrets, a value receiver copies them around the stack increasing exposure surface; minimize copies and zero out sensitive fields through pointer-receiver methods when done.

caseStudies.problem: Methods must mutate internal state reliably.
caseStudies.solution: These types use pointer receivers throughout (and must be passed by pointer, never copied).
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Callers must avoid copying the value; the vet tool flags copying a sync.Mutex.
caseStudies.lessons: Types with mutable state are pointer types by convention — copying them is a bug.

caseStudies.problem: Setters that silently did nothing because of value receivers.
caseStudies.solution: Standardized on pointer receivers for entities with state and added a linter rule against mixed receivers.
caseStudies.lessons: Consistency in receiver kind eliminates a whole bug class and clarifies which types are mutable.

keyTakeaways: A method is a function with a receiver: value receiver (func (t T)) works on a copy, pointer receiver (func (t *T)) works on the original.
Mutations through a value receiver are lost; use a pointer receiver whenever the method must change state or the struct is large.
Method set of T has only value-receiver methods; *T has both — so a pointer-receiver method means only *T satisfies an interface requiring it.
Go auto-takes the address on addressable values (c.Inc() -> (&c).Inc()), but you can't call a pointer-receiver method on a non-addressable value like a map element.
